source_text: Ἔτι δὲ περὶ Ἰουδαίων ἀποφαινόμενος ὁ Κέλσος φησίν· οὐδ᾿ εὐδοκιμεῖν παρὰ τῷ θεῷ καὶ στέργεσθαι διαφόρως τι τῶν ἄλλων τούτους εἰκὸς, καὶ πέμπεσθαι μόνοις αὐτοῖς ἐκεῖθεν ἀγγέλους, οἷον δή τινα μακάρων χώραν λαχοῦσιν· ὁρῶμεν γὰρ αὐτοὺς καὶ τὴν χώραν τίνων ἠξίωνται. ἐλέγξομεν οὖν καὶ τοῦτο, λέγοντες ὅτι τὸ εὐδοκιμηκέναι τὸ ἔθνος τοῦτο παρὰ θεῷ δηλοῦται καὶ ἐκ τοῦ τὸν ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεὸν καὶ ὑπὸ τῶν ἀλλοτρίων τῆς ἡμετέρας πίστεως Ἑβραίων καλεῖσθαι θεόν. καὶ ὡς εὐδοκιμοῦντές γε ὅσον οὐκ ἐγκατελείποντο, καίτοι γε ὀλίγοι τυγχάνοντες τὸν ἀριθμὸν, διετέλουν φρουρούμενοι ὑπὸ θείας δυνάμενως, ὡς μηδ᾿ ἐπὶ Ἀλεξάνδρου τοῦ Μακεδόνος παθεῖν τι αὐτοὺς ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ, καίτοι γε μὴ βουληθέντας διά τινας συνθήκας καὶ ὅρκους ἀναλαμβάνειν ὅπλα κατὰ τοῦ Δαρείου. τότε φασὶ καὶ τὸν Ἰουδαίων ἀρχιερέα ἐνδύντα τὴν ἱερατικὴν στολὴν προσκεκυνῆσθαι ὑπὸ τοῦ Ἀλεξάνδρου, φάσκοντος ὦφθαι αὐτῷ τούτῳ τῷ σχήματι † ἑωρακέναι τινὰ, ἐπαγγελλόμενον αὐτῷ „κατὰ τοὺς ὕπνους“ ὑποτάξειν τὴν Ἀσίαν ὅλην. ἡμεῖς οὖν οἱ Χριστιανοί φαμεν τὸ μὲν εὐδοκιμεῖν παρὰ τῷ θεῷ καὶ στέργεσθαι διαφόρως τι τῶν ἄλλων πάνυ ἐκείνοις συμβεβηκέναι, ταύτην δὲ τὴν οἰκονομίαν μεταβεβηκέναι καὶ τὴν χάριν ἐφ᾿ ἡμᾶς, μεταστήσαντος τὴν ἐν Ἰουδαίοις δύναμιν ἐπὶ τοὺς ἀπὸ τῶν ἐθνῶν πιστεύσαντας (αὐ) τῷ Ἰησοῦ. διὸ πολλὰ βουληθέντες Ῥωμαῖοι κατὰ Χριστιανῶν ἐπὶ τῷ κωλῦσαι αὐτοὺς ἔτι εἶναι οὐ δεδύνηνται· ἦν γὰρ ὑπερμαχοῦσα αὐτῶν θεία χεὶρ καὶ βουλομένη τὸν τοῦ θεοῦ λόγον ἀπὸ μιᾶς τῆς κατὰ τὴν Ἰουδαίαν γῆν γωνίας ἐπισπεῖραι ὅλῳ τῷ γένει τῶν ἀνθρώπων.
thought_title: God’s favour passes from the Jews to the Gentiles
pass_a_gloss: Still declaring (ἀποφαινόμενος) about Jews, Celsus says: 'nor is it likely (εἰκός) that these are in good repute (εὐδοκιμεῖν) with God and are loved (στέργεσθαι) differently in any way from the others, and that angels are sent (πέμπεσθαι) from there to them alone, as having obtained by lot (λαχοῦσιν) some land (χώραν) of the blessed (μακάρων); for we see them and the land, of what they have been deemed worthy (ἠξίωνται).' We shall refute (ἐλέγξομεν) this too, saying that this nation's having been in good repute with God is shown (δηλοῦται) also from the God over all being called (καλεῖσθαι) God of Hebrews even by those alien (ἀλλοτρίων) to our faith (πίστεως). And as being in good repute, so long as (ὅσον) they were not forsaken (ἐγκατελείποντο), although being few in number, they continued (διετέλουν) being guarded (φρουρούμενοι) by divine power, so as not even under Alexander the Macedonian to suffer anything from him, although not having wished, because of some agreements (συνθήκας) and oaths (ὅρκους), to take up (ἀναλαμβάνειν) arms against Darius. Then they say also the high priest (ἀρχιερέα) of Jews, having put on (ἐνδύντα) the priestly robe (ἱερατικὴν στολήν), was bowed down to (προσκεκυνῆσθαι) by Alexander, saying [that one] appeared (ὦφθαι) to him in this very form/dress (σχήματι) † to have seen someone, promising (ἐπαγγελλόμενον) him 'in sleep (κατὰ τοὺς ὕπνους)' to subject (ὑποτάξειν) all Asia. We Christians then say that being in good repute with God and being loved differently in any way from the others happened (συμβεβηκέναι) fully (πάνυ) to them, but this dispensation (οἰκονομίαν) and the grace (χάριν) have passed over (μεταβεβηκέναι) to us, Jesus having transferred (μεταστήσαντος) the power among Jews to those from the nations (ἐθνῶν) who believed in him. Therefore Romans, having wished many things against Christians for preventing (κωλῦσαι) them still to be, have not been able; for there was a divine hand (θεία χείρ) fighting for (ὑπερμαχοῦσα) them and wishing to sow (ἐπισπεῖραι) the word (λόγον) of God from one corner (γωνίας) of the Judean land to the whole race (γένει) of men.

choices.why: Celsus's last clause read as prolepsis: 'we see what they and their land have been thought worthy of' (removed a third object)
passive 'was bowed down to by Alexander' recast with Alexander as subject

pass_b_english: Pronouncing further on the Jews, Celsus says: “Nor is it likely that they stand in good repute with God, or are loved by Him in any way differently from others, or that angels are sent from there to them alone, as though they had been allotted some land of the blessed; for we see what they and their land have been thought worthy of.”

We shall refute this too. We say that this nation's good standing with God is shown also by the fact that the God over all is called the God of the Hebrews even by those who are strangers to our faith. And because they stood in good repute, so long as they were not forsaken, they continued to be guarded by divine power, though they were few in number. So it was that not even under Alexander of Macedon did they suffer anything at his hands, although, because of certain agreements and oaths, they had refused to take up arms against Darius. At that time, they say, when the high priest of the Jews had put on his priestly robe, Alexander even bowed down before him, saying that he had seen someone in this very dress who promised him “in his sleep” that he would make the whole of Asia subject to him (see Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 11.8.5).

We Christians, then, say that standing in good repute with God, and being loved in a way different from others, did indeed belong to them in full. But we say that this dispensation and the grace have passed over to us, since Jesus moved the power that was among the Jews to those from the Gentiles who believed in Him. That is why the Romans, though they wished to do much against the Christians to stop them existing any longer, have not been able to do so; for a divine hand was fighting for them, wishing to sow the word of God from one corner, the land of Judea, through the whole race of mankind.
notes: Source typo δυνάμενως read as δυνάμεως. Celsus's sentence 'we see them and the land, of what (τίνων) they have been deemed worthy' read as a prolepsis and rendered 'we see what they and their land have been thought worthy of' (ironic: their ruin). The passive 'the high priest ... was bowed down to by Alexander' recast with Alexander as subject; agency unchanged. τῶν ἐθνῶν rendered 'the Gentiles'. 'Called the God of the Hebrews even by strangers to our faith' probably refers to pagan invocations (compare Exodus 3:18, 'the God of the Hebrews', but no quotation is made, so not cited inline). The Alexander story (high priest Jaddua, refusal to break oaths to Darius, Alexander's dream) is in Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 11.8.3-5 (about 11.317-339); Koetschau marks 'in his sleep' (κατὰ τοὺς ὕπνους) as a quoted phrase; Origen says only 'they say'. Crux: φάσκοντος ὦφθαι αὐτῷ τούτῳ τῷ σχήματι † ἑωρακέναι τινά doubles the verb ('appeared' / 'had seen'); translated by the clear sense, 'he had seen someone in this very dress'. '(αὐ)τῷ Ἰησοῦ': Koetschau's supplement gives πιστεύσαντας αὐτῷ, with the genitive Ἰησοῦ as subject of μεταστήσαντος, hence 'since Jesus moved the power ... to those who believed in Him'. 'The word of God' here is the message preached, so lower-case 'word'. Section 51 continues to Celsus's charges against Moses and the Christians.
Open doubt (review): 5.50: the passage has a crux († ἑωρακέναι τινά). It is translated by its clear sense and the note records this. No owner action is needed unless the edition is collated again.
